svg.aria-label: Diagram: how AWS Signer separates a signing profile from the signatures it produces, and what each of its two revocation operations is documented to reach. AWS describes Signer as a fully managed code-signing service to ensure the trust and integrity of code, which manages the code-signing certificate's public and private keys and enables central management of the code-signing lifecycle, with CloudTrail integration to track who is generating code signatures. A signing profile is a unique Signer resource used to perform signing jobs, designating the signing platform, a platform ID and other platform-specific information, and it defines a trusted publisher whose signatures AWS Lambda verifies when code is deployed. Key custody is split by workflow: Signer manages the certificate and keys for AWS Lambda and container image workflows only, while for Internet of Things workflows the customer imports their own code signing certificate into AWS Certificate Manager, which means the sentence the signing key was disclosed describes two different incidents depending on platform. The profile carries a signature validity period specified in months, days or years whose default value is 135 months, stated by AWS as 11 years and 6 months, and up to 50 tags usable with tag-based resource policies to manage access to the profile. The central point concerns the two revocation operations and the asymmetry in what AWS documents about each. Revoking a signature has a documented verification outcome per platform: revoking the signature of an AWS Lambda deployment package invalidates it, causing it to fail Lambda signature checks in all Regions of the same partition, and revoking the signature of a container image causes validation to fail if deployment is attempted. Revoking a profile has exactly one documented statement of reach: once revoked, a signing profile can no longer be used for creating new signing jobs. That is forward-looking and says nothing about artifacts the profile has already signed, which on the day a signing key is disclosed are the entire problem. So if the requirement is that a specific artifact stop passing verification, the operation to use is RevokeSignature, because that is the one whose effect on verification is documented; revoking the profile stops the next signature rather than the last one, and the two are better treated as successive steps of one response than as alternatives. Profile revocation is also a timestamp rather than a switch, and each of its properties constrains the response. Revocation for a signing profile requires an effective start time in the past, the start time cannot be in the future, and the effective start time can be changed to an earlier date and time by repeating the revocation but cannot be revised to a later date and time. Three consequences follow: a revocation cannot be scheduled, it cannot be narrowed once made, and widening is the only correction available, so the recoverable direction is to revoke from later and walk it back rather than to start too early. Combined with the statement that revocation is an irreversible action recommended only for critical scenarios, this is a one-way ratchet into the past, and the discipline is to set the effective time from evidence about when exposure actually began rather than from caution. Making the time move only backwards is the right asymmetry, because narrowing a revocation would mean re-trusting artifacts previously declared untrusted, and the refusal to accept a future start time means the service will not represent a window in which a profile is both trusted and known bad. Revocation is addressed by profile version rather than by name alone: RevokeSigningProfile takes both a profile name and a profile version, and GetRevocationStatus takes a profile version ARN alongside the job ARN and the signature timestamp, which are the inputs a status is evaluated against. The retention rules are the clearest available statement of which object outlives the other, and they sit on a page about deletion. Signing profiles are automatically scheduled for deletion once canceled or revoked, and AWS retains the profile for an additional period explicitly to ensure that any existing signatures created with that profile have expired before it is deleted. The retention period is the profile's signature validity period plus 6 months, so with the 135 month default a canceled or revoked profile is deleted after 141 months, and a shorter validity period causes earlier deletion. For AWS IoT Device Management, canceled or revoked profiles have a retention period of 20 months. Signing jobs are automatically deleted 6 months after the generated signature expires, and for IoT Device Management the signing job retention period is also 20 months. Separately, revocation checks are valid for six months beyond the expiry of a signature, after which expired signatures fail on expiry checks instead, which bounds how long revocation state must be carried and means the long default validity rather than the revocation itself is what keeps that state alive for a decade. Reading the retention rule back, AWS keeps a revoked profile for up to 141 months because the signatures it produced are still in circulation, which establishes that signatures outlive the revocation of the profile that made them, while the user guide never states how such a signature verifies during that interval, and that gap is worth establishing with AWS for a given platform rather than assuming in either direction. The recommended actions are to use RevokeSignature for any artifact that must stop verifying, to treat profile revocation as the step that stops future signing, to set the signature validity period from how long artifacts actually live rather than inheriting the eleven-and-a-half-year default, to establish the exposure time from evidence before revoking because the effective time only moves earlier, to keep an artifact-to-profile-version inventory outside Signer because nothing in Signer maps versions to deployments, and to read CloudTrail before the incident since it tracks who is generating code signatures.
svg.title: Two revocation operations, and only one has a documented effect on verification
svg.text: Revoking the profile stops the next signature. It is not how you stop the last one.
AWS Signer — two similarly named operations, and the documentation is specific about only one of them.
THE PROFILE — the trusted publisher
Designates the signing platform and platform ID.
signature validity default: 135 months (11y 6m)
Keys: AWS holds them for Lambda + containers.
For IoT you import your own into ACM.
So “the key was disclosed” is two different incidents.
THE SIGNATURES — already out there
One per signing job. Attached to deployed
artifacts you no longer control.
Lambda “verifies signatures and package
integrity when code is deployed”.
These are the problem on the bad day.
RevokeSignature — outcome documented
Lambda package: “invalidates it, causing it to

text.tspan: fail Lambda signature checks in all Regions of

svg.text: the same partition”
Container image: “validation to fail if you
attempt to deploy the image”
This is the one that stops an artifact.
RevokeSigningProfile — reach unstated
“Once revoked, a signing profile can no
longer be used for creating new signing jobs.”
On already-signed artifacts: not stated.
It carries a timestamp, which exists to say
something about them — without saying what.
Establish this with AWS. Do not assume either way.
The effective time is a one-way ratchet into the past
“requires an effective start time in the past” · “cannot be in the future”
“can be changed to an earlier date and time by repeating the revocation, but cannot be revised to a later”
No scheduling. No narrowing. Widening is the only correction — so revoke from evidence, not from caution.
And the retention rule, on a page about deletion, is what gives the relationship away
“we retain the profile for an additional period of time to ensure that any existing signatures created with
that profile have expired before it is deleted”
validity 135 + 6 = 141 months · jobs deleted 6m after expiry · IoT: 20 months for both
AWS keeps the revoked profile for a decade because its signatures are still in circulation.
If an artifact must stop verifying, revoke its signature. Revoking the profile is how you stop the next one.
Then check every profile still carrying 135 months — an assertion held open into the late 2030s that nobody chose.
And keep the artifact-to-profile-version map. Signer answers “how do I revoke”; nothing in it answers “what did this sign”.
